references.text: The blind man was healed immediately and followed Jesus, praising God. A similar immediate healing is found in Luke 5:25, where the paralyzed man got up at once and went home while praising God.
In Luke 17:15, the Samaritan leper returns and praises God with a loud voice after being healed – the same pattern of healing followed by praise to God.
Psalm 146:8 says that "the Lord opens the eyes of the blind", which is fulfilled in Jesus' healing of the blind man.
The prophet Isaiah predicts that "the eyes of the blind shall be opened" in the messianic age (Isaiah 35:5). The healing of the blind man shows that this prophecy is fulfilled in Jesus' ministry.
The people's praise after seeing God's work reminds us of the shepherds in Luke 2:20, who praised God for all they had seen and heard.
In Luke 5:25–26, both the healed man and the crowd praised God after the healing of the paralyzed man, just as the blind man and all the people here praise God.
In Luke 7:16, the crowd was filled with awe and praised God after Jesus raised the widow's son at Nain – the same response from the people as in this verse.
The woman who had been bent over for eighteen years praised God when Jesus healed her (Luke 13:13), just as the blind man here praises God after receiving his sight.
The parallel account in Mark 10:52 tells of the same event where the blind man Bartimaeus is healed and follows Jesus on the way.
Matthew's parallel account in Matthew 20:34 also describes the healing of the blind men at Jericho, who then followed Jesus.
In Isaiah 42:7 it is prophesied that the Lord's servant will open the eyes of the blind. Jesus' healing of the blind man fulfills this messianic promise.
In Acts 4:21, the people praised God for what had happened – a parallel to the people's response here, where all who saw the healing gave glory to God.
